howbig

How big a sample do you need to find what changed in a network?

howbig gives power and sample-size calculations for differential network analysis: comparing two or more groups’ estimated graphical models to find the edges that differ. It is a network-native, method-aware analogue to pwr.

Its answers are empirical. They come from a large simulation study of differential network methods across sample sizes, feature counts, kinds of differential signal, and assumptions about the networks and data, plus an on-demand simulator for designs the study didn’t cover. howbig includes the nine methods from that study whose FDR-controlled calls could be scored. That evidence shows things a formula would hide:

  • Required sample sizes are large. With 250 features, the joint graphical lasso needs roughly 4,500 samples per group to recover 80% of the differential edges.
  • Method choice matters, and no method wins everywhere.
  • Some methods lose FDR control under some kinds of signal. howbig reports the false discovery rate a method actually achieves, next to its power, so that assumption is visible.

Installation 

# install.packages("remotes")
remotes::install_github("mljaniczek/howbig")

Looking up and interpolating the grid needs nothing else. To simulate a method you also need its package; dependencies = TRUE installs them all (several come from GitHub):

remotes::install_github("mljaniczek/howbig", dependencies = TRUE)

Example

You need four things: roughly how many features you’ll measure (p), a sample size per group (n), the method you plan to use, and what kind of change you expect between groups.

library(howbig)

power_for(p = 250, n = 1000, method = "JGL_BIC")
#> howbig power estimate  [in-grid]
#>   JGL_BIC | structural perturbation | p = 250, n = 1000
#>   Truly differential edges: ~50 of 31,125 pairs (0.16%)
#>   Sensitivity @ FDR 0.05:  0.60   (80% band 0.50–0.70)
#>   Achieved FDR:            0.059 ✓
#>   AUPR (threshold-free):   0.68
#>   based on 100 reps

The first result line shows how few edges actually differ: about 50 of 31,125 feature pairs in the simulated networks. Power is sensitivity: the fraction of those truly differential edges detected while controlling the false discovery rate at 5%. To go the other way, ask for the sample size that reaches a target power:

n_for(p = 250, power = 0.8, method = "JGL_BIC")
#> howbig sample-size estimate  [interpolated]
#>   JGL_BIC | structural perturbation | p = 250 | target power = 0.80 @ FDR 0.05
#>   Required per-group n:  4512

If you expect edge strengths to change rather than edges to appear or disappear, the picture changes. This method stops controlling its false discovery rate: about one in six of its calls is wrong.

power_for(p = 100, n = 1000, method = "JGL_BIC", perturbation = "magnitude")
#> howbig power estimate  [in-grid]
#>   JGL_BIC | magnitude perturbation | p = 100, n = 1000
#>   Truly differential edges: ~24 of 4,950 pairs (0.48%)
#>   Sensitivity @ FDR 0.05:  0.64   (80% band 0.37–0.84)
#>   Achieved FDR:            0.168 ⚠
#>   AUPR (threshold-free):   0.74
#>   based on 100 reps
#> note: achieved FDR 0.17 exceeds target 0.05 — this method is not
#>         calibrated here.

Unequal group sizes, and other assumptions about the networks and data, are in the grid at p = 100, n = 1000 per group on average:

power_for(p = 100, n = c(500, 1500), method = "JGL_BIC")
#> howbig power estimate  [in-grid]
#>   JGL_BIC | structural perturbation | p = 100, n = 500 / 1500
#>   Truly differential edges: ~45 of 4,950 pairs (0.92%)
#>   Sensitivity @ FDR 0.05:  0.62   (80% band 0.51–0.75)
#>   Achieved FDR:            0.047 ✓
#>   AUPR (threshold-free):   0.75
#>   based on 100 reps
power_for(p = 100, n = 1000, method = "JGL_BIC", scenario = "censored_25")
#> howbig power estimate  [in-grid]
#>   JGL_BIC | structural perturbation | p = 100, n = 1000 | scenario: censored_25
#>   Truly differential edges: ~45 of 4,950 pairs (0.92%)
#>   Sensitivity @ FDR 0.05:  0.65   (80% band 0.53–0.76)
#>   Achieved FDR:            0.092 ✓
#>   AUPR (threshold-free):   0.75
#>   based on 100 reps

howbig_methods() lists the nine methods and which ones can be simulated.

How answers are produced

Every answer states where it came from:

Provenance Meaning Speed
in-grid A precomputed simulation cell (typically 100 replicates) instant
interpolated Between grid cells along a swept axis instant
simulated A fresh simulation of your exact design minutes to hours
OFF-GRID Not answerable from the grid; howbig says why -

Designs the grid doesn’t cover are flagged, not guessed:

power_for(p = 150, n = 1500, method = "JGL_BIC")
#> howbig power estimate  [OFF-GRID]
#>   JGL_BIC | structural perturbation | p = 150, n = 1500
#>   Not available from the grid.
#> note: not answerable from the grid: (p = 150, n = 1500) is off the grid
#>         for the structural perturbation.
#> note: rerun with simulate = TRUE to simulate this design (slow; see
#>         ?simulate_power).

Rerunning with simulate = TRUE simulates that design, as do other unequal group sizes and FDR targets other than 5%. Each simulation estimates its runtime before it starts and refuses to start runs longer than max_minutes.
